items.stem: How had novels been easily available to the masses in Europe during nineteenth century? Explain with examples.
items.answer: Novels reached ordinary readers in nineteenth century Europe for three main reasons. The invention of the printing press and the technological advances that followed it made book production cheap and quick, so novels could be turned out in large numbers. Better transport and communication allowed copies to be sent to every part of Europe. Public and lending libraries were set up, so even people who could not buy a novel could borrow one. Together these developments put novels within easy reach of the masses.

items.answer: Many people were uneasy about print. First, they were apprehensive about the effect that easier access to the printed word and the wider circulation of books would have on people's minds. Second, they feared that if there was no control over what was printed and read, rebellious and irreligious thoughts might spread. Third, they believed that if that happened the authority of 'valuable' literature would be destroyed. So even those who welcomed print did so with fear.

items.stem: “The ‘Print Revolution’ had transformed the lives of people changing their relationship to information and knowledge.” Analyse the statement.
items.answer: The Print Revolution changed the way people related to information, knowledge, institutions and authority, and it opened up new ways of looking at things. Printing cut the cost of a book, because the time and labour needed for each copy came down and many copies could be produced with ease. Easy access to books also meant that even illiterate people could listen to sacred texts, folk tales and ballads being recited. Before the print revolution books were expensive and could not be produced in sufficient numbers; afterwards they reached far wider sections of people.

items.stem: Who took hand printing from China to Japan? Give two demerits of copying of manuscripts.
items.answer: Buddhist missionaries carried hand printing from China to Japan around 770 C.E. Two drawbacks of copying manuscripts were: (a) it was very expensive and time consuming, since a great deal of time was needed to copy anything; and (b) it demanded a great deal of labour from the person doing the copying.

items.stem: How did printing in Eruope shift from hand printing to mechanical printing? Did it prove a revolution in printing.? Explain. or How did print culture develop in Europe? Explain.
items.answer: In Europe books were at first produced by hand. In the late thirteenth century Marco Polo brought woodblock printing to Europe, but even then books were not produced in the numbers required. In the early phase of the fifteenth century Gutenberg developed the printing press, which brought a revolutionary change in book printing. Between CE 1450 and CE 1550 printing presses were set up in most European countries and the production of books boomed: about 200 lakh copies were printed in the second half of the fifteenth century, and the number rose to 2000 lakh in the sixteenth century. The shift from hand printing to mechanical printing therefore led to the print revolution.

items.stem: How did a new reading public emerged with the printed press? Explain. or How did Printing Press create a new reading public? Explain.
items.answer: The advent of the printed press changed the culture of reading. It reduced the cost of making a book and increased the number of books produced, so readership increased manifold. It created a new culture of reading: where earlier there had been a hearing public, now a reading public came into being. For those who could not read, printers began publishing popular ballads, folk tales and books with picture illustrations, and this gave rise to a new group of readers.

items.stem: Why mass literacy of workers in Europe was started in 19th century?
items.answer: Lending libraries had existed in Europe from the seventeenth century onwards, but in the nineteenth century these libraries became responsible for educating the lower middle class, white collar workers, artisans and similar groups. That is why mass literacy among workers began in Europe in the nineteenth century.

items.stem: Why literacy rate among women was increased in Europe in 19th century?
items.answer: The literacy rate among women rose in nineteenth century Europe because women writers began to write and women began to read those writings. Penny magazines were introduced for women, carrying manuals on proper behaviour and housekeeping. When novels were introduced in the nineteenth century, women became very important readers of those novels, and this reading habit raised female literacy.

items.stem: Give three arguments in support of the ‘print culture’.
items.answer: Print culture can be defended on three grounds. It made the ideas of enlightened thinkers popular, and their writing provided a critical commentary on tradition and superstition. It created a new world of debate and dialogue. And it made the public aware of the power of reason, so that people began to question all norms, values and institutions.

items.stem: A series of developments took place in the beginning of the twentieth century in print culture. What were they?
items.answer: At the beginning of the twentieth century printing improved in several ways. The methods of feeding paper into the press improved, the quality of printing plates became better, and automatic paper reels along with photoelectric controls of the colour register were introduced. The accumulation of these several individual mechanical improvements transformed the appearance of printed texts.

items.stem: When did the first printing press come to India and write a brief story of its growth?
items.answer: Before print, Indian texts were written on palm leaves or on handmade paper, and such books were sewn between wooden covers. The Portuguese missionaries came first, in the sixteenth century, bringing the press with them; they learnt the Konkani language and printed their teachings in it. The first Tamil book was printed in 1579 at Cochin by Catholics, and printing grew in India from these beginnings.

items.stem: Describe the role of nationalist newspapers in spreading national feelings among the people in the early 20th century.
items.answer: Nationalist newspapers grew in numbers in the early twentieth century. They reported on colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities. Attempts to throttle nationalist criticism in the papers only provoked militant protest. When Punjab revolutionaries were deported in 1907, Balgangadhar Tilak wrote about them with great sympathy in his Kesari, and this led to his imprisonment in 1908. In these ways the nationalist press spread national feeling among the people.

items.stem: Examine the role of missionaries in the growth of press in India.
items.answer: Missionaries played a very significant part in the growth of the press in India. The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid sixteenth century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani and printed several tracts, so that by 1674 about 50 books had been printed in the Konkani and Kanara languages. Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin and the first Malayalam book in 1713.

items.stem: “It is difficult to imagine a world without printed matter”. Justify the statement with suitable arguments.
items.answer: It is indeed very difficult to imagine such a world. Everywhere in our surroundings we find evidence of print, in books, journals, newspapers and prints of famous paintings. We also see printed material in the most everyday things, such as theatre programmes, official circulars, calendars, diaries, advertisements, cinema posters and government notifications. Print is therefore woven into ordinary life.

items.stem: Which values of print culture are responsible for the growth of nationalism in India?
items.answer: Print culture helped nationalism grow in India in three ways. It criticised the British policies of exploitation. It made people aware of the disadvantages of colonial rule. And it spread democratic ideas such as equality, fraternity and liberty among the people.

items.stem: Which values of French philosophers’ writings inspired the people of France to throw Monarchy?
items.answer: The writings of French philosophers such as Rousseau and Voltaire inspired democratic ideas all over the world. They laid stress on the value of equality for all, and they also advocated the importance of liberty and fraternity. These values inspired the people of France to throw off the monarchy.

items.stem: Write any three values due to which printed books became more accessible to common people.
items.answer: Printed books came within reach of common people because the cost of producing a book was low, because public libraries were opened, and because education spread.

items.stem: Why were manuscripts not used widely? Give three possible reasons.
items.answer: Manuscripts were not widely used for three reasons. They were not easy to handle. They were limited in number, since each copy had to be made by hand. And the style of writing differed from one copyist to another, with some hands being very untidy, so the manuscripts were hard to read.

items.stem: Explain the main features of the first printed Bible.
items.answer: The first printed book in Europe was the Gutenberg Bible, brought out in 1456. Until printing was invented books existed only in manuscript form, that is handwritten. Calligraphers copied them and they were mostly kept in the libraries of monasteries, so even people who could read had very little access to books, and most people of that time could neither read nor write. It has been estimated that during the first half of the fifteenth century there were only about 1,00,000 manuscripts in the whole of Europe.

items.stem: Which Asian country was the major producer of printed material in the 16th century and why? Give two reasons.
items.answer: China was the major producer of printed material in the sixteenth century. From AD 594 onwards books in China were printed by rubbing paper against inked woodblocks, and the Chinese made innovations in ink, in block printing and in movable clay type. They were the first to invent the art of printing, making wooden blocks to print letters. By the seventeenth century the uses of print had diversified and a new reading culture had developed alongside a new technology, with Shanghai becoming the main centre of the new print culture and catering to the west with its mechanical expertise in printing.

items.stem: Name the hub of the new print culture in China and describe it.
items.answer: Shanghai became the hub of the new print culture in China. In the late nineteenth century the western powers established mechanical printing presses there, and mechanical printing started in the city. Shanghai also began catering to the western style schools, and from hand printing there was a gradual shift to mechanical printing.

items.stem: Who was Erasmus? What were his ideas on the published books that were coming out?
items.answer: Erasmus was a Latin scholar and a Catholic reformer. He criticised the printing of books. He thought that most of the books being published were stupid, ignorant, slanderous, scandalous, raving, irreligious and seditious, and he held that such books devalued the books that were genuinely valuable.
items.concept: Religious debate and the fear of print

items.stem: “With the printing press, a new public emerged in Europe.” Justify the statement. or How did access to books create a new culture of reading? Examine.
items.answer: Access to books created a new culture of reading. Earlier reading was restricted to the elites, while common people relied only on oral culture, knowledge being transferred by word of mouth; now books were easily available. This transformed the lives of people, changing their relationship to information and knowledge and to institutions and authorities, influencing popular perception and opening up new ways of looking at things. In this way a new public emerged in Europe with the printing press.

items.stem: Why did the Roman Catholic Church begin to keep an Index of Prohibited Books from the mid 16th century? or Why did the Roman Church begin to maintain an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558?
items.answer: Menocchio, a miller in Italy, reinterpreted the message of the Bible and formulated his own view of God and Creation, which enraged the Roman Catholic Church. When the Roman Church began its inquisition to repress heretical ideas, Menocchio was hauled up twice and was ultimately executed. Troubled by such effects of popular reading and by this questioning of faith, the Roman Church imposed severe controls over publishers and booksellers and began to maintain an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.
items.concept: Religious debate and the fear of print

items.stem: Examine any three effects of Print culture on the French Revolution.
items.answer: Print culture prepared the ground for the French Revolution in three main ways. (1) It made the wide circulation of ideas possible: people who disagreed with established authority could now print and circulate their views, and through the printed message they persuaded others to think differently. (2) It speeded up the mobilisation of the masses behind the political ideals of freedom, liberty and justice for which the revolutionaries were fighting. (3) It exposed the draconian decisions of the monarchy and the higher estates, which awakened ordinary people and drew them into the revolution.

items.stem: How had the printing press created a new culture of reading in Europe? Explain with examples.
items.answer: With the printing press a new wave of print culture began in Europe. (1) Low cost of production: printing cut the cost of books because the time and labour needed for each copy fell sharply, so multiple copies could be made easily and books flooded the market for an ever-growing readership. (2) Accessibility of books: reading had earlier been restricted to the elites, while common people lived in an oral culture of sacred texts read out, ballads recited and folk tales narrated; cheap books now reached them. Before print, books were both expensive and too few in number, but now they could reach far wider sections of people. (3) Rising literacy: through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries literacy rates rose across most of Europe as churches of different denominations set up schools in villages, carrying literacy to peasants and artisans. As literacy and schools spread, Europe saw a virtual reading mania.

items.stem: “Print culture created the conditions within which French Revolution occurred.” Support the statement with suitable arguments.
items.answer: Print culture did create the conditions in which the French Revolution took place. (1) Print popularised the ideas of the Enlightenment thinkers. (2) These writers attacked the sacred authority of the Church and the despotic power of the state, eroding the legitimacy of a social order founded on tradition; Voltaire and Rousseau were widely read. (3) All values, norms and institutions came to be re-evaluated and discussed by a public that was inquisitive, critical and rational, so new ideas of social revolution came into being. (4) By the 1780s literature mocked royalty and criticised its morality, which fed hostile sentiment against the monarch.

items.stem: “Colonial administrators found ‘vernacular’ novels a valuable source of information on native life and customs.” Prove the statement by giving three evidences.
items.answer: Vernacular novels were useful to the colonial administration because they told the British about the Indian society they had to govern, a society of many communities and castes. (1) New novels such as ‘Indirabai’ described domestic life, showing how people dressed and what their religious beliefs and practices were; some of these books were translated into English by British administrators or Christian missionaries. (2) As outsiders the British knew very little about life inside Indian households, and the new novels in Indian languages carried exactly such descriptions of domestic life. (3) They recorded how people dressed, their forms of religious worship, their beliefs and their practices, which gave administrators first-hand information on native life and customs.

items.stem: Discuss in brief the development of printing culture in China.
items.answer: Printing culture in China developed in stages. (1) In the beginning China used hand printing, in which paper was rubbed against the inked surface of woodblocks. (2) In the sixteenth century the volume of print increased because civil service aspirants needed a growing number of textbooks. (3) With the blooming of urban culture in the seventeenth century the use of printed material grew once again. (4) Later China gradually moved from hand printing to mechanical printing.

items.stem: What is a manuscript ? Why were they not used widely ?
items.answer: A manuscript is a book or document written by hand — the author's original handwritten or typed copy, not printed. In ancient India most books existed only in manuscript form. They were not used widely because: (1) they were limited in number, so they were not accessible to all literate people; (2) they were not easy to handle, and carrying a big volume or an epic from one place to another was very difficult; (3) every individual's style of writing differs and some hands were very untidy, which made manuscripts hard to read.

items.stem: How were the books prepared in India in different languages before used of modern printing press ?
items.answer: Before modern printing technology reached India, books in the various Indian languages were prepared by hand. (1) Palm leaves or handmade paper were used to write the manuscript of a book. (2) Wooden covers were tied or sewn with the pages of the manuscript, made of bhojpatra and bark. (3) Calligraphy was practised to produce further copies of a manuscript. (4) Pages were duly illustrated, as can be seen in a page from the Diwan of Hafiz of 1824. (5) This way of making and writing books continued unbroken and exclusive until print was introduced in the late nineteenth century.

items.stem: How did press play an important role in spreading modern Indian nationalism in the second half of the 19th century ?
items.answer: The press was central to the spread of modern Indian nationalism. (a) It was the chief means of awakening the dormant people of India. (b) A large number of nationalist newspapers appeared during the second half of the nineteenth century. (c) In their columns official policies were constantly criticised and the Indian point of view was put forward; people were asked to unite and work for national welfare, and ideas of self-government, democracy and industrialisation were popularised. (d) The press also allowed nationalist workers living in different parts of the country to exchange views with one another.

items.stem: Explain the attitude of the British Government towards the Indian Press in the 19th century. Explain the main reasons for such an attitude.
items.answer: The British Government's attitude towards the Indian Press was one of control. (1) Restrictions were imposed on the Indian Press up to 1835 by Charles Metcalfe. (2) The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 curbed the freedom of the Indian Press, particularly of Indian-language newspapers. (3) The Act was repealed in 1882. (4) After that the press enjoyed considerable freedom for about twenty-five years. (5) Following the Swadeshi and Boycott movement of 1905, repressive press laws were again introduced in 1908 and 1910. The main reason for this attitude was to check the rising tide of Indian nationalism and of anti-British feeling among Indians.

items.stem: How did Martin Luther's writings bring reforms in religious field? Explain.
items.answer: Martin Luther (1483–1546) was a German monk, priest and professor of theology who wrote the ‘Ninety Five Theses’ criticising many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church. He taught that salvation is not earned by good deeds but received only as the free gift of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ as redeemer from sin. He believed in the infallibility of the Bible but challenged the authority of the Pope. Because his theses were printed and distributed widely in Germany — his translation of the New Testament sold 5000 copies within a few weeks — his ideas spread very fast. A National Church was established in Germany and prayers began to be held in German, which marked the beginning of the Reformation Movement in Europe.

items.stem: How did print culture affect women in the nineteenth century India ?
items.answer: Print culture changed the position of women considerably. (1) The lives and feelings of women began to be written about in particularly vivid and intense ways, and women's reading increased enormously in middle-class homes; liberal husbands and fathers began educating their womenfolk at home and sending them to school. (2) In East Bengal in the early nineteenth century Rashsundari Debi, a young married girl in a very orthodox household, learnt to read in the secrecy of her kitchen and later wrote her autobiography Amar Jiban, published in 1876 — the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language; a large part of it was devoted to the education of women. In the early twentieth century journals written for, and sometimes edited by, women became extremely popular.

items.stem:
What were the chief characteristics of the earliest print culture in Japan ? Explain any five.
or
Explain any three important characteristics of the print culture in Japan.
items.answer: The earliest print culture of Japan had these features. (1) Buddhist monasteries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan. (2) The oldest Japanese book printed in AD 868 is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra. (3) In medieval Japan poets and prose writers were regularly published and books were cheap and abundant. (4) The printing of visual material led to growing publishing practices; in the late eighteenth century, in the flourishing urban circles of Edo (Tokyo), illustrated collections of paintings depicted urban culture with its artists, courtesans and tea-house gatherings. (5) Books were also published on women, musical instruments, the tea ceremony, flower arrangement and proper etiquette.

items.stem:
How did the uses of print diversify in China by the 17th century ? Explain.
or
‘By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the use of print diversified.’ Give any three facts to support the statement.
or
How did a new reading culture bloom in China ? Explain.
items.answer: By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the uses of print became far more varied. (1) Print was no longer confined to scholars and officials. (2) Merchants used print in their everyday work as they collected trade information, and reading turned into a leisure habit. (3) Rich women began to read, and many of them began publishing their poetry and plays. (4) The wives of scholar-officials published their works, and courtesans wrote about their own lives. Thus a new and much wider reading culture bloomed in China.

items.stem: How had the earliest printing technology developed in the world ? Explain.
items.answer: The earliest print technology grew up in East Asia. (1) It was developed in China, Japan and Korea. (2) Up to the sixth century print was used only by scholar-officials. (3) Buddhist monasteries then introduced hand-printing technology more widely. (4) Marco Polo carried woodblock printing from China to Italy. (5) From this beginning came the printing press, whose invention proved a great miracle in spreading knowledge.

items.stem: Give three methods by which printed books became more accessible to common people.
items.answer: Printed books reached common people through the following means. (1) The cost of producing books fell. (2) Books were printed in very large numbers. (3) Public libraries, book stalls and shops opened, lending or selling books at very little profit, and the habit of borrowing books from book banks made books still more accessible. (4) The spread of education, the spare time available to women at home and the desire to spend leisure in reading all widened the reading public.

items.stem: Why were the printed books popular even among illiterate people ?
items.answer: Printed books were popular even with those who could not read. (1) Common people lived in a world of oral culture in which sacred texts were read out, ballads recited and folk tales narrated, so knowledge reached illiterate people by ear. (2) Illiterate people heard a story collectively or saw a performance, and many were attracted by the beautiful pictures printed in the books. (3) Even those who could not read could enjoy listening to books being read out, so printers began publishing popular ballads and folk tales, profusely illustrated with pictures, which were then sung and recited at gatherings in villages and in taverns in towns.

items.stem: What do you understand by Print Revolution? How did the idea of the scientists and philosophers become more accessible to common man after beginning of this revolution in Europe ?
items.answer: The Print Revolution means the transformation brought about by modern printing technology, which covers not only printing but also the sizing and cutting of paper for the printed pages and the binding of those pages under a stiff or soft cover, so producing whole books, magazines and newspapers with or without illustrations. Before printing, and even in the early stage of woodblock printing, books could not be produced anywhere near as fast as they are today by rotary machines that print newspapers or by modern automatic electronic printers; printed material can now be ready for sale or distribution almost as soon as printing is complete. Because of this, the ideas of scientists such as Sir Isaac Newton, Einstein and Galileo, and of philosophers such as Thomas Paine, Voltaire and Jean Jacques Rousseau, could be read easily in books, so common people far beyond the authors' own circles benefited from their ideas, laws and rules, all fairly explained in print.

items.stem: Invention of printing press by Johann Gutenberg led to revolution in the realm of ideas. Justify.
items.answer: The Gutenberg Press was the breakthrough in print technology. It was at Strasbourg in Germany that Johann Gutenberg developed the first known printing press in the 1430s. He made metal types for each of the 26 characters of the Roman alphabet and devised a way of moving them about so as to compose different words of the text; this became the moveable type printing machine and remained the basic print technology for the next 300 years. Books could now be produced far faster than when each print block had to be carved out of wood by hand — the Gutenberg press could print 250 sheets on one side in an hour. The first book printed by Gutenberg was the Bible, and it took three years to print 180 copies. By multiplying books in this way the press spread ideas rapidly and so brought about a revolution in the realm of ideas.

items.stem: Why was there a strong criticism from some scholars against indiscriminate publication of all types of books ?
items.answer: Scholars feared print because it could not be controlled. (1) Their major fear was that if there was no control over what was printed and read, rebellious and irreligious thoughts might spread. (2) Priests, monks, bishops and the monarch regarded writers and artists as dangerous to their authority and influence over the people, since their own value would fall once things they alone knew became known to all. (3) An example from Europe is Manocchio, a miller in Italy, who acquired the ability to re-interpret the message of the Bible; he was warned twice and finally the inquisition (Trial Court) pronounced the death sentence against him. An Indian example is that many conservative Hindus and Muslims placed restrictions on the reading of books by women and by vulnerable sections of society, allowing only upper and middle class and caste people to read.

items.stem: “Pariksha Guru is considered landmark in the history of Hindi novel.” Justify the statement with suitable arguments.
items.answer: Pariksha Guru, the first Hindi novel, tells the story of the extravagance of Hindu bankers and traders, and its theme is that modern life should be embraced without abandoning Indian culture. (1) It cautioned young men of well-to-do families about the ill effects of bad company. (2) It showed how to live a practical life that preserves traditional values in honour and dignity. (3) It advised children to read the newspaper. (4) The author emphasised that modernity should be embraced without giving up middle class values. (5) The novel tries to teach the reader the ‘right way’ to live, expecting ‘sensible men’ to be worldly-wise and practical, rooted in the values of their own tradition and culture, and to live with dignity and honour. (6) Its characters attempt to bridge two different worlds: they take to new agricultural technology, modernise trading practices and change the use of Indian languages so that they can carry both Western science and Indian wisdom. Because no earlier novel had attempted this, Pariksha Guru is rightly called a landmark in the history of the Hindi novel.

items.stem: Distinguish between the themes of ‘Pride and Prejudice’ and ‘Jane Eyre’ novels written by Jane Austen and Charlotte Bronte respectively.
items.answer: For both novelists the main idea of the novel centres on women, but the two writers hold different ideas and opinions. (1) The first line of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice states that “It is a universally acknowledged truth, that a single man in possession of good fortune, must be in want of a wife”; Austen’s observation shows that women of that society were always preoccupied with the perception of marriage and money. Her novels give a glimpse of the world of women in genteel rural society in early-nineteenth-century Britain and make us think about a society that encouraged women to look for ‘good’ marriages and wealthy or propertied husbands, so her main characters typify that society. (2) In Charlotte Bronte’s Jane Eyre, young Jane is shown as independent and assertive at a time when girls were expected to be quiet and well behaved; at the age of ten she protests against the hypocrisy of her elders with startling bluntness. Bronte dealt with women who broke the established norms of society before adjusting to them, and such stories allowed women readers to sympathise with rebellious actions. Thus Austen mirrors the marriage-and-money world of genteel women, while Bronte projects the rebellious, self-assertive woman.

items.stem: Explain the impact of print culture on the religious reforms in India during nineteenth century.
items.answer: (1) Print led to intense controversies between social and religious reformers and Hindu orthodoxy over matters like widow immolation, monotheism, the Brahmanical priestly system and idolatry. (2) With the coming of print, ulama feared that colonial rulers would encourage conversion; to counter this they used cheap lithographic presses, published Persian and Urdu translations of holy scriptures and printed religious newspapers and tracts. (3) Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821 and Hindu orthodoxy commissioned the Samachar Chandrika to oppose his opinions. (4) In Bengal, as the debate developed, tracts and newspapers proliferated and circulated a variety of arguments. (5) A number of Muslim sects and seminaries appeared, each with a different interpretation of faith, each keen on enlarging its following and countering the influence of its opponents. Print therefore turned religious reform into a public, argumentative movement that reached far beyond the elite.

items.stem:
“Oral culture and print culture were complimentary to each other.” Justify the statement with any three suitable arguments.
or
How did print bring the reading public and hearing public closer ? Explain.
or
Highlight any three circumstances that led to the intermingling of the hearing culture and the reading culture.
items.answer: (1) Earlier, reading was restricted to the elites. (2) With the printing press books could reach wider sections of society; if earlier there was only a hearing public, now a reading public came into being. (3) Publishers had to keep in mind the wider reach of printed books, because even those who could not read could enjoy listening to books being read out. (4) So printers began publishing popular ballads and folk tales, and such books were profusely illustrated with pictures. (5) These were then sung and recited at gatherings in villages and in taverns in towns, so the line that separated the oral and reading cultures became blurred. (6) In this way the hearing public and the reading public became intermingled, and the two cultures supported each other.

items.stem: Describe any five strategies developed by the printers and publishers in the 19th century to sell their products.
items.answer: In the nineteenth century printers and publishers continuously developed new strategies to sell their products. (1) Periodicals serialised famous novels, which gave birth to a particular way of writing novels; in 1863 Charles Dickens’s ‘Pickwick Papers’ was serialised in a magazine, and magazines were attractive to readers because they were illustrated and cheap, so readers bought them eagerly. (2) In 1920s England popular works were sold in cheap series called the Shilling Series. (3) The dust cover or book jacket was introduced to make the book more attractive to readers. (4) Books were printed on the offset press, which could print in six colours at a time. (5) To sustain buying during the Great Depression of the 1930s, publishers brought out cheap paperback editions, which soon became a big hit. These devices kept books affordable and desirable and widened the market for print.

items.stem: How did the invention of Printing Press help the emergence of Renaissance ?
items.answer: The printing press increased the number of books, newspapers, magazines, pamphlets and other reading material, and with more of these things more people gained easy access to knowledge. The new knowledge increased rational thinking and helped greatly in reducing superstition and orthodoxy in religion as well as in society. Very soon the new atmosphere began to appear in the political life of several countries of Europe and other parts of the world. It was a Renaissance in terms of material progress although premature in terms of enlightenment; its consequences were apparent in the use and misuse of new skills, expertise, efficiency and authority. Creative and destructive powers alike found support in the technological change brought by print. Human minds of every temperament — genteel, aggressive or dull — took help from print technology. The Renaissance was thus seen in technological change, mechanical development and the industrial age, even as it left society divided into two classes, capitalists and proletariats.

items.stem: How did print culture affect women in the nineteenth century India ? Explain
items.answer: The number of women readers swelled enormously in middle class homes, for the following reasons. (1) Many magazines and books were written mainly for women and published. (2) Print culture gave women some amount of freedom to read and to develop their own views on various issues, especially those concerning women. (3) Issues such as women’s education, widowhood and widow re-marriage came to be liberally debated in print. (4) Women novelists such as Jane Austen and the Bronte sisters in Europe and Kailashbasini Debi and Pandita Ramabai in India represented a new type of woman — a woman with the power to think and the ability to act with determination. (5) Girls, especially from the middle classes, began to enrol in school in large numbers. In a word, print culture heralded the arrival of a new woman.

items.stem: Describe the progress of print in Japan.
items.answer: (1) Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan around 768–770 C.E. The oldest Japanese book, printed in 868 C.E., is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations; pictures were also printed on textiles, playing cards and paper money. (2) In medieval Japan poets and prose writers were regularly published, and books were cheap and abundant. (3) Printing of visual material led to interesting publishing practices: in the late eighteenth century, in the flourishing urban circles at Edo (later to be known as Tokyo), illustrated collections of paintings depicted an elegant urban culture involving artists, courtesans and teahouse gatherings. (4) Libraries and bookstores were packed with hand-printed material of various types — books on women, musical instruments, calculations, the tea ceremony, flower arrangements, proper etiquette, cooking and famous places. Print thus grew from a religious craft into the basis of a wide popular urban culture in Japan.

items.stem:
Discuss the position of printing technology in 17th century China. How was it affected by western technology in 19th century ?
or
How did the uses of print technology develop in China by the 17th century ? Explain.
items.answer: Development of printing technology in seventeenth century China: (1) By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the uses of print diversified. Print was no longer used just by scholars and officials; merchants also used print in their everyday life as they collected trade information. (2) Reading increasingly became a leisure activity, and the new readership preferred fictional narratives, poetry, autobiographies, anthologies of literary masterpieces and romantic plays. (3) Rich women began to read, and many women began publishing their poetry and plays; wives of scholar-officials published their works and courtesans wrote about their lives. Effect of western technology in nineteenth century China: (1) Since hand printing had started in China, books began reaching a public that included children, both boys and girls, youths, adults and senior people, and all shared in the exchange of scientific, theological and practical thought; bureaucrats now came through examinations such as the civil service examinations held there. (2) School textbooks on the western education system came in a glut, which many felt polluted Chinese culture, though they also accommodated socialisation once the Western powers established their roots in China.

items.stem:
How did the print material of Europe affected the rise of nationalism in India ?
or
How did print culture contribute to growth of nationalism in India ?
items.answer: (1) Western education had been widening the horizon of understanding of a number of things among Indians. (2) It gave educated Indians a rational, secular, democratic and national outlook; western thinkers like Rousseau, Paine and John Stuart Mill greatly influenced the Indian intelligentsia. (3) Italian nationalists like Garibaldi, Mazzini and Cavour also greatly influenced them. (4) When educated Indians came in contact with western education it opened their eyes. (5) Translation of western literature into Indian languages proved highly useful in bringing about a new awakening both in the cities and in the villages. (6) Revolutions like the American War of Independence and the French Revolution gave the thoughts of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity to the whole world. (7) The spirit of nationalism and patriotism made Indians forget their differences and inspired them to smash the wheels of oppression and exploitation that had been crushing their very existence for several centuries.

items.stem: What were the important features of European literature ? How did it help in spreading new or progressive ideas in the continent ?
items.answer: The important features of European literature were as follows. (1) The new literary works of different European authors, poets and languages helped greatly in promoting new and progressive ideas; this literature was concerned with social injustice and with nationalism. (2) The writers of modern Europe tried their best to promote realism and to avoid meagre idealism; realism was reflected very well in the works of Charles Dickens and Thomas Hardy in England, Leo Tolstoy, Ivan Turgenev and Dostoevsky in Russia, and Balzac, Flaubert, Emile Zola and Anatole France in France. (3) Human suffering during World War I increased enormously; these events of pathos stirred sensitive people, who put their feelings on paper (palm leaves or handmade), and such people were known as playwrights, dramatists, poets, philosophers, scientists and researchers. (4) Renowned authors like James Joyce (Ireland), Marcel Proust (France), Virginia Woolf (England) and Scott Fitzgerald (USA) made their fortune and glory with the help of advanced printing technology. (5) The exuberance and overflow of cheap books like chapbooks and the Bibliotheque Bleue gave pain to scholars such as Erasmus, who felt such books deceived the eye and pumped ignorance into the minds of adolescents all over Europe. (6) European literature also covered the countryside (folk tales, songs, stories, fables), schooling, training, course books, books on entertainment, and books on science and theology such as Gutenberg’s Bible. Together these writings carried new and progressive ideas across the continent.

items.stem: How did the printing and writing of Indian History during the late 19th and early 20th centuries prove a mixed blessing for the Indian society ?
items.answer: (a) Indians lost confidence in their own capacity for self-government. Many British officials and writers of the time constantly advanced the thesis that Indians had never been able to rule themselves in the past, that the Hindus and Muslims had always fought each other, that Indians were destined to be ruled by foreigners, and that their religion and social life were degraded and uncivilised, making them unfit for democracy or even self-government. (b) Many nationalist leaders pointed to the cultural heritage of India with pride and referred the critics to the political achievements of rulers like Ashoka and Chandragupta Vikramaditya; some nationalists went to the extreme of glorifying India’s past uncritically, ignoring its weaknesses and backwardness. (c) Great harm was done, in particular, by the tendency to look up only to the heritage of ancient India while ignoring the equally great achievements of the medieval period. (d) This encouraged the growth of communal sentiments among the Muslims, who began looking to the history of the Arabs and the Turks for cultural and historical inspiration while their feet were living in Indian land. Printed history therefore both awakened national pride and sowed communal division — a mixed blessing.

items.stem: Describe main aims and suggestions of the Press Commission of 1952 C.E.
items.answer: The Government of India appointed a Press Commission in 1952. It consisted of 11 members and its Chairman was Justice G. S. Rajadhyaksha; it submitted its report in 1954. Its aims were: (1) to safeguard the freedom of the Press; (2) to censure objectionable types of journalistic conduct; (3) to encourage a sense of responsibility and public service among journalists; (4) to keep under review developments likely to restrict the supply and fair distribution of news of public interest and importance; (5) to improve methods of recruitment and training for the journalistic profession; and (6) to study developments in the Press and suggest measures to check the concentration of the Press in a few hands. Suggestions: the Commission suggested banning cross-word puzzle competitions in newspapers and periodicals, and recommended that not more than 40% of the total space should be covered by advertisements; this put teeth into the income side of printing and kept printers submissive. Conclusion: most of the suggestions of this Commission were accepted by the Government of India and incorporated in law.

items.stem: The books are considered an effective means of spreading progress and enlightenment. Justify the statement how ?
items.answer: (1) All the great revolutions — the Protestant Reformation, the Union of England and Scotland in 1707, the Declaration of American Independence and the like — took place when print culture spread in Europe and the Americas, because books made people able to understand the importance of freedom. (2) Playwrights, poets and authors like Shakespeare, Mathew Arnold, Abul Fazal, Ayodhya Singh Upadhyay, Mulk Raj Anand, William Blake, Bhartrihari and Bankim Chandra Chatterjee were products of that period. (3) Cartoons, caricatures and several types of painting indicate the sensitivity of human minds and bring out even the most concealed human emotions. (4) So far as enlightenment is concerned, it remained confined to philosophers, anthropologists and philanthropists, because the viruses of domination, imperialism and ego stood in the way of understanding the European West. Books therefore carried progress and enlightenment to whole societies, even if the deepest enlightenment reached only a few.

items.stem: Discuss briefly the growth of modern press in 19th century in India.
items.answer: The growth of the modern press in nineteenth century India was as follows. (1) The growth of the press started with the arrival of print culture in India and happened in the later years of the nineteenth century. (2) Prior to the arrival of print culture in India, palm leaves or handmade paper were used for writing and copying manuscripts, and such books were bound with wooden sheets. (3) The first print in India was the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine edited by James Augustus Hickey; thereafter its Bangla edition was also published by some Bengali scholars under the guidance of Raja Ram Mohan Roy. (4) Other newspapers followed this trend — Amrit Bazar Patrika, Yugantar (Bengali) and Kesari (Marathi); watchwords like Vande Mataram became a jewel in every mouth during India’s freedom struggle. (5) Sambad Kaumudi (1821) by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, the Samachar Chandrika, Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar (Persian newspapers), the Bombay Samachar and the Gujarat Newspaper were some of the other forms taken by print culture and print technology.

items.stem:
What were the effects of the spread of print culture for poor people in nineteenth century India ?
or
What was the impact of print culture on the poor people of India during the 19th century?
items.answer: The effects of the spread of print culture for poor people in nineteenth century India were: (1) large scale printing maintained reasonable prices for books, so the poor too enjoyed reading; (2) many of them got employment in printing presses and print shops; (3) the spread of print culture helped to restrict excessive drinking among the poor, to bring literacy, to give way to the shackles of the caste system and to propagate the message of nationalism; (4) they became aware of national, international and local news through cheap printed material; (5) with the Vernacular Press, nationalist ideas made a home in the minds of poor people; and (6) caste discrimination was brought up through print culture, which associated poor people with the nationalist freedom struggle.

This is how Mercier describes the impact of the printed word, and the power of reading in one of his books:

‘Anyone who had seen me reading would have compared me to a man dying of thirst who was gulping down some fresh, pure water…. Lighting my lamp with extraordinary caution, I threw myself hungrily into the reading. An easy eloquence, effortless and animated, carried me from one page to the next without my noticing it. A clock struck off the hours in the silence of the shadows, and I heard nothing. My lamp began to run out of oil and produced only a pale light, but still I read on. I could not even take out time to raise the wick for fear of interrupting my pleasure. How those new ideas rushed into my brain! How my intelligence adopted them!’

Questions:
1. How does the passage reflect the immersive nature of reading of Mercier?
2. Why did Mercier describe himself as a virtual writer?
3. How did reading influence Mercier’s intellectual capacity and his engagement with new concepts? Explain in any two points.
items.answer:
1. The thirst, the hunger and the complete focus that Mercier describes — reading on by a failing lamp, hearing nothing as the clock struck the hours — reflect the immersive nature of his reading.
2. He gave voice to the people, putting into words the ideas and beliefs he had himself absorbed from the spread of printed material; in that sense he wrote what his reading had made of him.
3. Reading influenced his intellectual capacity and his engagement with new concepts because (a) his heroes are transformed by the act of reading, and (b) it brought enlightenment and destroyed the basis of despotism. Thus reading remade both Mercier’s mind and, through him, his readers’ minds.

Gutenberg was the son of a merchant and grew up on a large agricultural estate. From his childhood, he had seen wine and olive presses. Subsequently, he learnt the art of polishing stones, became a master goldsmith, and also acquired the expertise to create lead moulds used for making trinkets. Drawing on this knowledge, Gutenberg adapted existing technology to design his innovation. The olive press provided the model for the printing press, and moulds were used for casting the metal types for the letters of the alphabet. By 1448, Gutenberg perfected the system. The first book he printed was the Bible. About 180 copies were printed and it took three years to produce them. By the standards of the time this was fast production.

Questions:
1. Who was Gutenberg?
2. What were some of the professional skills acquired by Gutenberg?
3. What contribution was made by Gutenberg in the field of press?
items.answer:
1. Gutenberg was a German inventor, printer and goldsmith who invented the first known printing press in the 1430s.
2. He learnt the art of polishing stones and gained expertise in creating the lead moulds used for making trinkets; he became a master goldsmith and designed several jewels.
3. He gave the world the printing press. Adapting the olive press as his model, he used cast metal types for the letters of the alphabet; the first book printed by this technology was the Bible, of which more than 180 copies were produced.

New forms of popular literature appeared in print, targeting new audiences. Booksellers employed peddlars who roamed around villages, carrying little books for sale. There were almanacs or ritual calendars, along with ballads and folktales. But other forms of reading matters, largely for entertainment, began to reach ordinary readers as well.

In England, penny chapbooks were carried by petty peddlars known as chapmen, and sold for a penny, so that even the poor could buy them. In France, were the ‘Biliotheque Bleue’, which were low-priced small books printed on poor quality paper, and bound in cheap blue covers. Then there were the romances, printed on four to six pages, and the more substantial ‘histories’ printed on four to six pages and the more substantial ‘histories’ which were stories about the past. Books were of various sizes, serving many different purposes and interests.

Questions:
1. Evaluate briefly the term ‘Chapbook’.
2. Write a key difference between Biliotheque Bleue and Chapbook.
3. Comment on the new forms of literature that were introduced in Europe to attract new readers.
items.answer:
1. Chapbooks were pocket-size books sold by travelling peddlars called chapmen, priced at a penny so that even the poor could buy them.
2. The ‘Biliotheque Bleue’ were low-priced small books printed in France on poor quality paper and bound in cheap blue covers; chapbooks, by contrast, were pocket-size books published in England, which became popular from the time of the sixteenth century print revolution.
3. The new forms of literature introduced in Europe to attract new readers were almanacs or ritual calendars along with ballads and folktales; in England chapbooks carried by petty peddlers and sold for a penny; and in France the low-priced Biliotheque Bleue — besides romances and the more substantial ‘histories’.

The earliest kind of print technology was developed in China, Japan and Korea. This was a system of hand printing. From AD 594 onwards, books in China were printed by rubbing paper - also invented there - against the inked surface of woodblocks. As both sides of the thin, porous sheet could not be printed, the traditional Chinese ‘accordion book’ was folded and stitched at the side. Superbly skilled craftsmen could duplicate, with remarkable accuracy, the beauty of calligraphy. The imperial state in China was, for a very long time, the major producer of printed material. China possessed a huge bureaucratic system which recruited its personnel through civil service examinations. Textbooks for this examination were printed in vast numbers under the sponsorship of the imperial state. From the sixteenth century, the number of examination candidates went up and that increased the volume of print.

Questions:
1. Name the nations where the earliest print technology was developed.
2. How the books were printed in China from 594 AD?
3. Discuss the relationship between the bureaucratic system of China and the production of printed materials.
items.answer:
1. The earliest print technology was developed in China, Japan and Korea.
2. Books in China were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks — a system of hand printing.
3. China had a large bureaucratic system whose personnel were recruited through civil service examinations. Textbooks for these examinations were printed in large numbers under imperial sponsorship, and from the sixteenth century the rising number of candidates raised the demand for printed textbooks, so the bureaucracy itself drove the growth of print.

The English language press did not grow in India till quite late even though the English East India Company began to import presses from the late seventeenth century.

From 1780, James Augustus Hickey began to edit the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine that described itself as ‘a commercial paper open to all, but influenced by none’. So it was private English enterprise, proud of its independence from colonial influence, that began English printing in India. Hickey published a lot of advertisements, including those that related to the import and sale of slaves. But he also published a lot of gossip about the Company’s senior officials in India. Enraged by this, Governor-General Warren Hastings persecuted Hickey, and encouraged the publication of officially sanctioned newspapers that could counter the flow of information that damaged the image of the colonial government. By the close of the eighteenth century, a number of newspapers and journals appeared in print. There were Indians, too, who began to publish Indian newspapers. The first to appear was the weekly Bengal Gazette, brought out by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy.

Questions:
1. Which weekly magazine described itself as ‘a commercial paper open to all, but influenced by none’.
2. Why Governor-General warren Hastings persecuted James Hickey? What did he encourage regarding publication?
3. What did happen by the eighteenth century regard printing?
items.answer:
1. The Bengal Gazette, the weekly magazine James Augustus Hickey began to edit from 1780, described itself as ‘a commercial paper open to all, but influenced by none’.
2. Hickey published many advertisements, including those relating to the import and sale of slaves, but he also published a great deal of gossip about the Company’s senior officials in India — which is why Governor-General Warren Hastings persecuted him. Hastings then encouraged the publication of officially sanctioned newspapers that could counter the flow of information damaging the image of the colonial government.
3. By the close of the eighteenth century a number of newspapers and journals appeared in print, and Indians too began to publish Indian newspapers — the first being the weekly Bengal Gazette brought out by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohan Roy.

From the late nineteenth century, issues of caste discrimination began to be written about in many printed tracts and essays. Jyotiba Phule, the Maratha pioneer of low caste’ protest movements, wrote about the injustices of the caste system in his Gulamgiri (1871). In the twentieth century, B.R. Ambedkar in Maharashtra and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker in Madras, better known as Periyar, wrote powerfully on caste and their writings were read by people all over India.

Workers in factories were too overworked and lacked the education to write much about their experiences. But Kashibaba, a Kanpur millworker, wrote and published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938 to show the links between caste and class exploitation. The poems of another Kanpur millworker, who wrote under the name of Sudarshan Chakr between 1935 and 1955, were brought together and published in a collection called Sacchi Kavitayan. By the 1930s, Bangalore cotton millworkers set up libraries to educate themselves, following the example of Bombay workers. These were sponsored by social reformers who tried to restrict excessive drinking among them, to bring literacy and, sometimes, to propagate the message of nationalism.

After the revolt of 1857, the attitude to freedom of the press changed. Enraged Englishmen demanded a clamp down on the ‘native’ press. As vernacular newspapers became assertively nationalist, the colonial government began debating measures of stringent control. In 1878, the Vernacular Press Act was passed, modelled on the Irish Press Laws. It provided the government with extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press.

Questions:
1. Who was Jyotiba Phule?
2. How did the message of nationalism propagate?
3. What do you mean by the Vernacular Press Act?
items.answer:
1. Jyotiba Phule was the Maratha pioneer of the low caste protest movement and a social reformer, who wrote about the injustices of the caste system in his Gulamgiri (1871).
2. Social reformers sponsored libraries set up to educate mill and factory workers. Through these they also tried to restrict excessive drinking among the workers, to bring literacy and, sometimes, to propagate the message of nationalism.
3. The Vernacular Press Act, passed in 1878 and modelled on the Irish Press Laws, was enacted to curtail the freedom of the Indian press and to prevent the expression of criticism of British policies in British India, giving the government extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press.
